script_json.title: Enrolling on an evening course
script_json.scenario: A man telephones the enrolments office of a community college to join an evening course; the officer takes his details and explains the practical arrangements.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part one. You will hear a telephone conversation between a man and an enrolments officer at a community college. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Good afternoon, Northgate Community College, enrolments. Rachel speaking.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Oh, hello. I'm ringing about the evening classes — the autumn ones. Is it too late to sign up?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Not at all. We've still got places on most of them. Have you studied with us before?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: No, this'd be my first time.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, then I'll need to put you on the system. Could I take your surname first?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: It's Okafor.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Sorry, would you mind spelling that for me?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Of course. O-K-A-F-O-R. Okafor.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Lovely, thank you. And your first name?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Daniel.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Thanks, Daniel. And could I have an address?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Yes, it's twenty-seven Bellfield Road. Bellfield — that's B-E-L-L-F-I-E-L-D — Road, Northgate.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Twenty-seven Bellfield Road. Got it. And are you working at the moment? I only ask because a few of our courses have a daytime group as well.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Yes, I'm an electrician, so honestly the evening is the only thing that works for me.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's no problem at all — nearly all the craft courses run in the evening. Can I also ask how you heard about us? We have to report it for our funding.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Erm, I think I saw something on your website first. No — actually, that's not right. I picked up one of your brochures in the library.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The library, perfect. They're very good to us. So, did you have a particular course in mind?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Well, I was hoping to do Introduction to Photography, but a mate of mine said it's already full.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: I'm afraid he's right — photography filled up in about a week. There's still room on Introduction to Bookbinding, though, and it's the same tutor.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Bookbinding. Do you know, that actually sounds better. Put me down for that one, please.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Introduction to Bookbinding. Now, that course runs twice a week — there's a Tuesday group and a Thursday group.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Tuesday would be — hmm, no, sorry, I've got five-a-side on Tuesdays. Thursday, please.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Thursday it is. I'll email a confirmation across once we're finished.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, Daniel, just a few practical things. The Thursday group meets in the Beech Building, on the first floor.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: And what time does it start? I don't finish work until six.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You'll be fine. We used to begin at half past six, but we pushed it back — classes now start at 6.45 and run through until nine.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: 6.45. That gives me time to get across town. And what about the fee?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, the full fee for a ten-week term is 96 pounds.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Ah. Right.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: But there's a reduced rate for anyone living in the borough, and Bellfield Road is well inside it, so you'll pay 86 pounds a term.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That's a relief. Can I pay it in instalments?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You can — two payments. One when you enrol, and one at half term.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Great. And is there anything I need to buy beforehand? Tools, or a kit of some sort?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: No, all the tools stay in the workshop. People often turn up with their own scissors and a bone folder, but we supply all of that. The one thing I would say is bring an apron, because the glue does splash.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: An apron. I'll dig one out of the van.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And do bring your enrolment reference to the first session. It'll be at the bottom of the email.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Will do. Can I ask what happens if I have to miss a week? We sometimes get called out at short notice.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's fine — just let the tutor know. She puts a short summary of each session on the course page, so you can catch up before the next one. As long as you make eight of the ten, you'll get your certificate.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Oh, there's a certificate? I wasn't expecting that.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: There is, and there's a little exhibition on the last Thursday of term — families are welcome. Most people bring whatever they've made.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That sounds lovely. Right — oh, one last thing: parking. Is there anywhere to leave the van?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: There is, yes. The main car park is reserved for staff during the day, and at weekends it's closed for the market — but from six in the evening it's free for anyone on a course.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Perfect. That's everything, I think. Thanks very much for your help, Rachel.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You're welcome, Daniel. We'll see you on the fifth of October.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part one.

title: Welcome talk at the Fairhaven Leisure Centre

script_json.title: Welcome talk at the Fairhaven Leisure Centre
script_json.scenario: A duty manager gives an introductory talk to a group of new members of a leisure centre: the history of the building, the practical arrangements, and which part of the centre suits which kind of member.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part two. You will hear a duty manager giving a welcome talk to a group of new members at a leisure centre. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to fifteen.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Hi everyone, and welcome to Fairhaven. My name's Marissa, I'm one of the duty managers here, and this little talk is what we do instead of a guided tour — mainly because the tour takes forty minutes and the coffee is free for the next twenty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, a bit of history first, because somebody always asks what this building used to be. Most people guess it was already a swimming pool. It wasn't. And it wasn't the old cinema either — that was two streets over, where the car showroom is now.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: This was the town's bus depot, right up until 2019.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You can still see it, actually. That high curved roof over the main pool is the original depot roof, and the green tiles in the entrance hall came straight out of the old ticket office.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right. The practical things. Your membership card is also your locker key — tap it on the locker door to lock, tap it again to open. If you lose it, a replacement is four pounds, so please try not to.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You really don't need to bring much with you. Towels are free to borrow: just ask at reception and drop them in the basket by the exit on your way out.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Swimming costumes and goggles you would have to buy, I'm afraid, and the vending machine by the door is honestly a last resort.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Parking is the thing I get asked about most. When we first opened we only had ninety spaces and it was chaos every evening, but the extension last spring took us up to 120, plus twelve accessible bays right beside the door.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The barrier reads your number plate, so there's nothing for you to do. The first three hours are free as long as your card has been scanned inside the building.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, the pool timetable is printed on the back of your welcome sheet, but let me flag one thing, because people get this wrong all the time. If you don't like a crowded pool, everybody assumes Saturday morning is the quiet one.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It really isn't — Saturday morning is when the swimming club has all six lanes.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Our quiet swim sessions are on Sunday mornings, seven until ten. Lane ropes out, no whistles, and the lights are kept low. It's the nicest two hours of the week, in my opinion.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And bookings. Anything with an instructor — classes, the squash courts, the climbing wall — has to be booked through the app. Not the website.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The website is only for memberships, and it will cheerfully tell you a class is available when it's been full since Tuesday. So: the app.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Booking opens a week ahead at seven in the morning, and yes, the popular classes do go in about two minutes.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now look at questions sixteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: OK. The last thing I want to do is point a few of you in the right direction, because Fairhaven is a big building and it's very easy to end up doing exactly the same thing every week.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So — if you've never actually learnt to swim, and a lot of adults haven't, there's nothing unusual about it at all, please don't start in the main pool. It's two metres deep at the shallow end and it's full of people doing lengths.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Go to the learner pool instead, round behind the changing rooms. It's warmer, it's chest-deep the whole way along, and there's an instructor in the water every weekday evening.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: If you're training for something, on the other hand — and we've got a lot of members doing the half marathon in October — the treadmills upstairs will do you no favours whatsoever. Use the outdoor track.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It's floodlit until nine, it's properly measured, and on Tuesday evenings there's a group that runs intervals together.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Then there are people who simply cannot make themselves exercise alone. I'm one of them, honestly. If that's you, the studio is where you want to be.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: There are eighteen classes a week in there, everything from spin to very gentle chair yoga, and you'll be in a room with thirty other people who also didn't want to come.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: If you're bringing small children in, particularly at lunchtime, then it's the family café on the first floor. There's a play corner, the floor is designed to be dropped on, and nobody minds the noise.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The roof terrace is lovely, but that's the one place we ask people to keep the tables adult-only until two o'clock.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And if what you actually want is to try something you have genuinely never done before — the climbing wall. You do need a twenty-minute induction first, that's free, and after that you can book it like anything else.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: One of our members started at seventy-one, so I don't want to hear about your knees.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's me finished. Grab a coffee, have a wander round, and if you get lost — and everyone gets lost near the squash courts — just ask anybody in a red top.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part two.

script_json.title: Tutorial: an air-quality field-work project
script_json.scenario: Two geography students discuss their field-work proposal on high-street air quality with their tutor, who criticises their measurement plan and questionnaire before they divide up the remaining tasks.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part three. You will hear two geography students, Priya and Callum, discussing a field-work project with their tutor, Doctor Hallam. First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Come in, both of you. Right — the field-work proposal. I've read it. Before we get into the detail, tell me what happened to the river study, because that's what you pitched to me last month.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Yes, sorry, we did change it. We were going to sample water quality along the Cray, but when we went to book the meters, the second-year group had already taken all four of them for the whole of March.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: We did ask whether we could borrow a set from the university across town, but their technician said no. Insurance, apparently.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: That's a shame. Honestly, though, it's not a disaster — you'd have spent half your word count explaining the chemistry. So now it's air quality on the high street.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's right. Nitrogen dioxide, using diffusion tubes, and then a short questionnaire with pedestrians about whether they actually notice the traffic.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Mm. I like the questionnaire. What worries me is the measurement side. Talk me through where the tubes are going.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Six sites. Three at the pedestrianised end by the market, and three at the junction outside the station.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Six sites is fine. That isn't what I mean. Look at your timings — you've got every tube going up at nine in the morning and coming down at five the same afternoon.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Well, that's a full working day.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: It is. But it's one working day. Nitrogen dioxide doesn't sit still — you'll catch a rush-hour spike, a lunchtime dip, and if it happens to rain on your Tuesday you'll have measured the weather, not the traffic.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Diffusion tubes are designed to run for a fortnight.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: So we just leave them up for two weeks.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Two weeks minimum, and take them down at the same hour you put them up. That one change will do more for your marks than anything else in this proposal.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's fine by us — it actually makes life easier. We were dreading a fourteen-hour day in February.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Now. The questionnaire. How long is it at the moment?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Twenty-two questions.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Twenty-two. And how long did it take you to fill in?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: About seven minutes.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: And you wrote it. Nobody standing outside a chemist's in February is going to give you seven minutes.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: We could always put it online instead — a QR code in the shop windows.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: You could, but then you lose the one thing that makes it field work: you, standing there, watching who walks past. No — cut it. Five questions, one side of paper, and you'll get four times the responses.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Five. All right. We'd keep the two about perceived noise, and the one about how they travelled in.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Can I raise the other thing that's bothering me? I'm not convinced we'll get a representative sample at all. Half the people on that high street on a weekday are commuters walking from the station car park to the platform.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: They don't live in the borough, they've got no particular view about local air quality, and they're in a hurry.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: That's a genuinely good observation — and it's a finding, not a problem. Make 'where have you come from today' your first question, and then you can report your results by group.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Residents notice it, commuters don't: that's a far more interesting paragraph than anything you'd get out of twenty-two questions.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Should we be comparing our numbers with anything official?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: You should — and that's actually where I'd start, before you order a single tube. The council publishes an annual air-quality report, and there's been a permanent monitoring station on that junction since 2016.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Read the last three years of it, take their baseline, then design your sites so they tell us something the station can't.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: The journal literature can wait until you write your discussion, and you've clearly read the department handbook already — your risk assessment was the best I've seen this term.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now look at questions twenty-six to thirty.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Right. Let's divide the work up, because you've got three weeks and a reading week sitting in the middle of them. Who's doing what?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: I'll take the tubes. I've already emailed the lab and they've got twelve spare, so I'll book those out on Monday and get them labelled.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Good. And the council data?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That's me. My cousin works in the planning office — which doesn't help in the slightest, but at least I know who to ask. I'll request the raw monthly figures rather than the summary table.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Ask by email, so you've got a record of what you requested. And the risk assessment will need redoing now the tubes are staying up for a fortnight — different hazards, and you'll be working up a ladder on the lamp posts.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That's mine as well, then. I wrote the first one, so I may as well.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Fine. The questionnaire itself?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: We thought we'd write that one together, actually. We disagree about half the wording, so it's probably better if we argue it out now rather than in the write-up.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: It is. And we'll both pilot it — ten people each, on the Saturday.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: That's the right instinct. And the mapping? I want to see your sites on a proper base map, not a screenshot of an online one.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: I'll do the maps. I took the mapping module last year, so I can get the traffic-flow layer in underneath as well.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: And I'll draft the method section while she's doing that.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Send me one page a week. Not a polished draft — one page, in whatever state it's in. That's the only thing that keeps a project like this on schedule.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Thank you. That's really helpful.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: See you next Tuesday.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part three.

title: Lecture: street trees and the modern city

script_json.title: Lecture: street trees and the modern city
script_json.scenario: A university lecture on the history of urban street trees, the species chosen for city streets, what cities now expect trees to do, and why so many street trees die young.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part four. You will hear part of a lecture about street trees in cities. You now have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Good morning. Last week we looked at parks, which are essentially pieces of countryside that a city has agreed to keep. This week I want to talk about something much stranger: the tree that lives in the pavement. The street tree.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And I want to start with where the idea came from, because it isn't ancient. Medieval cities had orchards inside the walls, and they had a tree on the green, but they did not line their streets with trees.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The deliberate planted avenue is a Renaissance invention, and the first city to do it at any scale was Paris, in the sixteen hundreds.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: London followed a century later, and Berlin later still, and in both cases the model was explicitly the Parisian one — a straight road, a double row of limes, and a view at the end of it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, why? If you ask people today why the Victorians planted street trees, they'll usually say for beauty, or for the birds. Neither is right, and the second one would have puzzled them enormously.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The reason given in almost every council minute of the eighteen sixties is shade. Shade for pedestrians, shade for horses, and shade for the shop fronts, because sunlight faded the goods in the window. It's a completely practical argument.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: There was a second argument, though, and it's the one I find most interesting, because it was wrong. Before germ theory was accepted, the great fear in cities was bad air — miasma. And trees, it was believed, cleaned that air and therefore prevented disease.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: There are pamphlets from the cholera years that recommend planting as a public-health measure, in the same paragraph as widening the sewers.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: They were wrong about the mechanism, obviously. But we'll come back to whether they were wrong about the outcome.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right — species. If you walk down almost any older street in a British or French city and look up, you're probably looking at one tree: the London plane. And the plane was not chosen because anybody thought it was beautiful. It was chosen because it survives.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It tolerates industrial air, it doesn't mind having its roots in rubble, and it sheds its bark in plates, which takes the soot off with it — a self-cleaning tree, in a city that burned coal.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Where the plane failed, cities moved to limes, and then to a much wider palette after the disease outbreaks of the last thirty years taught us what a monoculture costs.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: But survival is exactly where the modern problem lies. The average street tree planted today in a British city has a life expectancy, in some surveys, of under twenty years. A plane in a park will live for three hundred.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So what kills them? Not, usually, pollution, and not vandalism, although both get blamed. The single commonest cause of early death is compaction.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The soil under a pavement is compacted to something close to the density of concrete, deliberately, because that's what stops the paving from moving.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Roots cannot get air or water through it, and a tree that cannot root simply declines for a decade and then dies in a dry summer.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Which brings us to what we now ask these trees to do — and we ask a great deal more of them than the Victorians did.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The first thing is temperature. A street with a closed canopy can be five degrees cooler at head height, on a summer afternoon, than the identical street next to it without trees.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: In a city with an ageing population and no air conditioning, that is not a comfort question, it's a mortality question — which is, I think, the sense in which the miasma pamphlets accidentally got it right.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The second is water. A mature canopy intercepts rainfall before it reaches the drains, and the fashionable engineering solution now is to plant trees in structural soil that doubles as a storm-water reservoir. The tree becomes part of the drainage system.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the third is money, which is where management comes in. Once you can put a figure on the cooling and the drainage and the particulates, a tree stops being decoration on the balance sheet and becomes an asset — and assets have to be replaced.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Most local authorities are now required to publish a replanting programme, setting out how many trees they will put back for each one they take down.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The public dimension of this is worth a moment. When Melbourne mapped its urban forest, it gave every single tree an identification number and, as an afterthought, an email address, so that residents could report damage.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: What happened instead is that people wrote to the trees. Thousands of letters — some of them, I promise you, love letters. Which tells you something useful about consent: it is much harder to fell a tree that people have written to.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, targets, and then I'll stop. The figure you'll see in most strategy documents is a canopy-cover target of thirty per cent — that is, thirty per cent of the city's surface shaded when you look down on it from above. Very few European cities are there.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The typical British figure is around sixteen.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the constraint on getting there is changing. For a century the limiting factor on urban planting was pollution, and we solved a great deal of that. The limiting factor now, on every species list I've read in the last five years, is drought.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The question is no longer what a tree can breathe, it's what it can drink.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Next week we'll look at how you actually value one of these things in cash terms, and I'll ask you to bring the two valuation papers from the reading list.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part four. You now have half a minute to check your answers.
